extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and practitioners in information visualization / data graphics
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Edward Tufte's principles for the visual display of quantitative information: rules about graphical integrity, data-ink/data-density, chartjunk, small multiples, color use, layering, and other design heuristics to create truthful, efficient, and informative graphics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical excellence is the well-designed presentation of interesting data — complex ideas communicated with clarity, precision and efficiency; it gives the viewer the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time with the least ink in the smallest space and is nearly always multivariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should communicate many ideas quickly and efficiently, be multivariate where appropriate, and must tell the truth about the data. Emphasize substance, statistics, and design together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Your graphic should tell the truth about your data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure baselines, scales, and contexts are correct and visible; avoid misleading truncation or omission of relevant ranges; make choices that do not distort the data's message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart integrity: baseline, scale, context
rubrics_metrics.description: Always show appropriate baseline (where's 0?), correct scale, and relevant context for the data being presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid chopped y-axes that exaggerate changes; show full scale or broader temporal/contextual range when needed; when a short-range view is necessary, explicitly indicate it and provide context elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch size coding (area/volume vs linear encodings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful when encoding data with area or volume—height/width/area/volume do not scale the same way; visual attribute value should be directly proportional to the data attribute value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid representing values by circle width or diameter (people misinterpret area/volume); prefer linear encodings (position or length) when accurate magnitude comparisons are required. Use dot plots instead of bars when ranges down to zero are problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure misrepresentation (Lie factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify graphical distortion: Lie factor = Size of effect shown in graphic / Size of effect in data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute lie factor to detect exaggeration (example in slides shows large lie factor values). The visual effect should be proportional to the actual data effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize data-ink ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Data-ink ratio = data ink / total ink used in graphic. Maximize the proportion of ink devoted to the non-redundant display of data-information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Above all else, show the data. Erase non-data-ink and redundant data-ink, revise and edit graphics to remove gratuitous marks. Reduce ornamentation that does not convey data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize data density
rubrics_metrics.description: Data density = number of entries in data matrix / area of data graphic. Maximize data density (within reason) to give context and credibility to statistical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display as much relevant information as reasonably possible so viewers can compare parts of the data at a glance. Avoid low-information designs that hide what is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chartjunk
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extraneous visual elements that detract from the message; 'chartjunk' is content-free decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove unnecessary ornamentation, clip art, heavy background patterns, or gratuitous 3D effects that obscure the data. However, note nuance: modest embellishment can sometimes improve memorability or preference depending on purpose and data complexity — purpose matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize multifunctioning graphical elements (macro/micro readings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphical elements that serve both data-information and design/structural functions so that elements simultaneously convey macro (overview) and micro (detail) readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design marks that provide overall patterns at a glance while also supporting detailed inspection; examples include purposeful layering and combined representations that do not sacrifice clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small multiples
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat visually similar graphical elements nearby (small multiples) rather than scattering related graphics far apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small multiples enable easy comparison across conditions or categories by placing similar charts together (examples: 23-hour pollution charts, chromosome comparisons, consumer reports). Use consistent scales/encodings across the multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparklines and small repeated graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sparklines — very small, high-density line graphs — when appropriate to show trends compactly and repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sparklines are useful for embedding many tiny trend indicators inline with text or tables; they are an extension of the small-multiples principle for minimalist trend displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show mechanism, process, dynamics, and causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphics should, when relevant, show cause-and-effect, dynamics, or mechanisms rather than only static summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design visuals to make causal relationships and processes visible where the analysis task requires it (e.g., sequences, timelines, annotated process diagrams). Use narrative sequencing and appropriate encodings to make causality evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape flatland (represent multivariate data appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that data are multivariate; escaping 'flatland' does not necessarily mean defaulting to 3D projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual encodings and layouts that reveal multivariate structure (small multiples, layering, color, position), but avoid gratuitous 3D that harms interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize layering and separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use layering and separation of graphical elements to make information combine multiplicatively (1+1=3 or more) when done well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply visual layering (foreground/background, contrast, emphasis) to separate concerns, highlight important series, and support multiple levels of detail; be cautious — layering can be good or bad depending on execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize narratives of space and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell a story of position and chronology through visual elements; use spatial and temporal narratives to organize data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design charts to communicate positional relationships and temporal progressions clearly (timetables, sequences, spatial maps) so viewers can follow a narrative implied by the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content is king
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality, relevance and integrity of content are fundamental; the visual design should reflect the analysis task and integrate text, chart, graphic, and map into a coherent narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First make sure the data and analysis are appropriate; then choose formats and designs that support the analytic goal (description, exploration, tabulation, or decoration). Integrate verbal/statistical descriptions with visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph and chart tips (legends, grids, labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separate legends and keys — put that information in the graphic; make grids, labeling, and other ancillary marks very faint so they recede into the background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed labeling directly where possible (direct-labeling of series), use faint gridlines, unify legend information in-place to reduce eye movements and cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using color effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: "Above all, do no harm" — color is subtle and complex; use color to label, to measure, to represent/imitate reality, or to enliven/decorate but with great care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive or confusing color palettes; ensure color choices support task (e.g., categorical vs sequential palettes), consider color vision deficiencies, use color to add informative dimensions not merely decoration, and avoid making screens look like 'video games'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guides for enhancing visual quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Attractive displays of statistical information have a properly chosen format and design; use words, numbers and drawing together; reflect balance, proportion, and relevant scale; display accessible complexity; often have a narrative quality; be drawn professionally; avoid content-free decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose formats that match the analytic question, combine textual annotation with visuals, maintain professional production quality (typography, alignment), and ensure the graphic communicates a coherent story without gratuitous ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical displays should (comprehensive checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphics should: show the data; induce the viewer to think about substance rather than methodology or technology; avoid distorting what the data have to say; present many numbers in a small space; make large data sets coherent; encourage the eye to compare pieces of data; reveal data at several levels of detail; serve a clear purpose; be integrated with statistical and verbal descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to evaluate whether a graphic fulfills its role: clarity, non-distortion, density/coherence, comparability, multiple-detail levels, explicit purpose (description/exploration/tabulation/decoration), and close integration with analysis/narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid information overload by design (clutter is a design failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clutter and confusion are failures of design, not attributes of information; stripping detail is not always correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate quantity of information with overload; instead, design to present detail clearly. Over-simplifying by removing relevant detail can make a graphic less informative and more ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability and embellishment nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Color and recognizable objects can enhance memorability, and embellished charts were found in some studies to be recalled better and preferred by participants — but memorability is only one utility dimension and may not be the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider purpose: if memorability or recall is important, modest embellishment might help; if precise interpretation is primary, prefer clarity and simplicity. Tailor embellishment to data complexity and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baselines & alternative encodings (dot plots, redesign examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: When bars spanning down to zero produce misleading impressions or when range is large, consider alternative encodings such as dot plots and show more of the underlying data/context in redesigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dot plots for cases with large ranges or when area encodings distort perception; redesign examples (news graphics before/after) illustrate making baselines and heights meaningful and showing more data.
